title: Runtime schema & feature-flag strategy for zero-downtime private upgrades
content:
Purpose:
This note documents a pragmatic approach for performing runtime upgrades in private (VPC/on-prem) deployments with minimal or zero-downtime. It focuses on two hard-to-get-right parts: evolving KV/persistent state schemas and using feature flags to gate new control-plane/runtime behaviors. Also includes practical Terraform considerations for stateful infra changes and a fallback recipe for rapid rollback.

Scope and goals:
- Support rolling upgrades of runtime and control plane components in private deployments without requiring long maintenance windows.
- Enable multi-version reads/writes for critical KV-backed artifacts (model metadata, shard manifests, routing table entries).
- Use feature flags to separate code rollout from behavior activation.
- Provide Terraform module notes to avoid state drift and preserve on-prem idempotency.
- Produce clear verification steps and a short rollback path.

Assumptions and prerequisites:
- Customers run Redwood Private with an immutable image model for runtime nodes and a control plane that can be upgraded independently.
- KV store = Consul or etcd (or compatible hosted DB) with support for atomic updates and TTLs.
- Access to metrics/tracing (Prometheus, Grafana, Jaeger) and an out-of-band admin channel (SSH bastion or management plane).
- Terraform used for infra provisioning; state is stored remotely (S3/GCS with locking) for on-prem gateways or a supported backend.

High-level strategy:
1) Preflight: detect capabilities, pin conservative defaults.
2) Make schema changes backward-compatible (read-old, write-new or dual-write) and deploy schema-aware runtime code.
3) Rollout runtime binary in canary waves while keeping behavior gated by feature flags.
4) Gradually flip flags once telemetry validates correctness.
5) Decommission old schema paths and cleanup after a safe delay.

Detailed plan
A. Preflight checklist (run before any infra or code changes):
- Inventory: list keys/prefixes used by runtime and control plane. Export sample payloads for each key.
- Baseline tests: run local compatibility tests against current KV snapshot (see linked test harness).
- Capacity check: confirm KV cluster storage and request limits for absorbing dual-write traffic.
- Backup: export KV snapshot + Terraform state snapshot. Tag snapshots with deployment id.
- Communication: notify customer ops and agree on maintenance window fallback steps.

B. Schema migration patterns (choose one per artifact):
1) Read-new / write-old (adapter pattern)
  - Behavior: new runtime reads the new shape if present, otherwise falls back to old shape. New runtime continues writing in the old shape until flag flips.
  - When to use: safe when new fields are additive and consumers can ignore unknown fields.
2) Dual-write (write both v1 and v2 keys/prefixes)
  - Behavior: runtime writes both representations atomically when possible. Readers migrate to new path on read success.
  - When to use: when the old consumers cannot be easily changed but we need immediate availability on the new format.
3) Adapter shim (migration service)
  - Behavior: lightweight migration service listens for writes, emits transformed copies to the new keyspace asynchronously.
  - When to use: large backfills or heavy schema changes where dual-write on hot code path is undesirable.

C. Feature-flag rollout strategy
- Flag semantics: boolean + rollout percentage + metadata (safe-timestamp). Flags stored in control plane and propagated to nodes via existing config stream.
- Phases: off -> small canary (1-5 nodes) -> regional canary (10-20% traffic) -> majority -> global ON.
- Safety gates: automated rollback when error-rate > threshold or token latency regresses more than X p50/p95.
- Fast disable: flag toggle must be sub-second; ensure control-plane propagation latency is understood.

D. Runtime upgrade waves (example):
1) Build and register new image/version, ensure it passes smoke tests in isolated lab.
2) Canary wave: replace 1-2 nodes per cluster (or 1 instance in each AZ) with new image, keep feature flags OFF.
3) Enable internal health checks and metrics collection for new nodes. Observe for 30-60 minutes.
4) If stable, enable feature flag for canary nodes to test schema read/write behavior.
5) Expand canary to 10-20% using weighted routing; monitor.
6) If OK, perform full rolling update in groups (10-25% at a time) while gating feature flag activation per group.

E. Terraform module notes (stateful infra):
- Avoid automatic resource renames: explicit lifecycle "prevent_destroy" on critical data volumes/kv clusters.
- Introduce new resources in additive manner: terraform apply should create new resources rather than mutating existing ones in-place when possible.
- Use data resources to read existing IDs instead of hardcoding.
- State handling: always run terraform plan and a secondary diff tool (k8s manifests or API) before apply in prod.
- Example pattern for KV storage change (text only):
  - Step 1: Add new resource with distinct name (kv_cluster_v2).
  - Step 2: Deploy migration adapter to copy data from kv_cluster_v1 -> kv_cluster_v2 while both are active.
  - Step 3: Switch runtime config to point to kv_cluster_v2 behind a DNS alias.
  - Step 4: Remove kv_cluster_v1 once traffic is fully migrated and backups verified.
- Locking: enforce remote state locking (dynamodb/consul lock) for any apply that touches KV or networking.

F. Rollback recipe (fast path)
- If canary nodes fail after feature flag ON: immediately toggle flag OFF.
- If code-level regressions happen: roll back images in the canary group to previous image and set flag OFF cluster-wide.
- If schema write caused unrecoverable corruption: restore KV from snapshot (preflight backup) and re-run adapter with corrected transform.
- Runbook commands (examples to keep in vault):
  - Toggle flag (control-plane CLI): rwdctl flags set --name runtime-kv-v2 --value false --env customerX
  - Rollback image: rwdctl nodes replace --cluster customerX-prod --old-image redwood/runtime:2024.11.1 --new-image redwood/runtime:2024.10.4 --group canary
  - Restore KV snapshot: kvcli restore --snapshot s3://backups/customerX/kv-20241115.tar.gz --cluster kv-cluster

G. Observability and verification
- Canary success criteria: error-rate < baseline + 0.5% and token p95 latency regression < 10% over 30m window.
- Post-write verification: background job polls migrated keys and validates checksums for a 24h window.
- End-to-end smoke tests: ingestion -> inference -> traceable spans present and no missing context (requires trace sampling to be ON for canary).
- Dashboards to monitor: per-route latency, per-model cache hit rate, kv write latency, leader election frequency, disk utilization.

H. Cleanup and hard migration steps
- After 14-30 days of stable operation, schedule a cleanup run: remove old keyspace shards or deprecated payload fields.
- Ensure audit log contains the timeline and data supporting removal decisions.
- Update Terraform modules to remove deprecated resources as a final step only after backups and regulatory retention periods are satisfied.

I. Known risks and mitigations
- Risk: Dual-write increases KV QPS and might push the cluster past limits. Mitigation: throttle writer, scale KV cluster ahead of migration, use backpressure-aware writer.
- Risk: Feature flags not propagated quickly due to network isolation. Mitigation: pre-warm config endpoints, verify polling/streaming behavior in staging with similar network restrictions.
- Risk: Terraform state drift between operator teams. Mitigation: centralize apply rights, require plan sign-off and automated diffs.

Testing matrix (minimal):
- Unit tests for schema adapter and serializer changes.
- Integration tests that spin up minified KV + runtime, exercise read-new/write-old and dual-write flows.
- Chaos tests: kill leader, partition a node during migration, and ensure clients fallback gracefully.
- Load test: simulate expected QPS with dual-write enabled to validate latency envelope.

Recommended quick checklist for an upgrade window
- T-minus 72h: run inventory, snapshot KV, review Terraform plan.
- T-minus 24h: deploy migration adapter to staging, smoke test.
- T-minus 2h: apply Terraform changes that are additive only.
- T-minus 30m: bring canary nodes with new image up (flags OFF).
- T-plus 60m: enable canary-level flag; observe.
- T-plus 6-12h: expand rollout groups incrementally per stability.
- Post-migration +1w: continuous read verification job results review.

Contacts and escalation:

- Secondary: Diego Alvarez — diego.alvarez@redwood.ai
- SRE on-call: (link to rota)

Appendix: example Terraform snippet (illustrative, not copy-paste for prod)
- # add new cluster resource idempotently
- resource "kv_cluster" "v2" {
    name = "${var.cluster_name}-v2"
    replicas = var.kv_replicas
    storage_gb = var.kv_storage_gb
  }
- data "kv_cluster" "current" {
    name = var.cluster_name
  }

Notes for future improvements:
- Introduce a built-in migration API in the runtime to declare schema transforms and run them server-side with idempotency guarantees.
- Add a migration simulator tool that replays production traces against a schema adapter to estimate migration impact before touching live KV.

Open questions:
- Do we want to support automatic coalescing of dual-writes into a single transaction for some KV backends? (requires backend support)
- How long to retain old keyspace before cleanup (compliance-dependent)?

End of document.
